title: Quadratic Equations
intro: Quadratic equations are a cornerstone of SAT Advanced Math. This chapter covers the standard form, solving by factoring, the square-root method, completing the square and the quadratic formula. Read each topic, try the problems with the hint ladder, then take the 8-question topic test.

items.name: Zero-product rule
items.formula: if AB = 0 then A = 0 or B = 0

topics.name: Standard Form
topics.details: The standard form of a quadratic equation is ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. Putting an equation into this form — by moving every term to one side so the other side is 0 — is the first step before factoring or using the quadratic formula. Here a is the leading coefficient, b the linear coefficient and c the constant. Identifying a, b and c correctly (with their signs) is essential, because the quadratic formula and the discriminant both depend on them. The SAT frequently gives a quadratic in a rearranged form and expects you to standardise it first.

solved.solution: Bring all terms to one side: x² − 4x − 5 = 0.
There is no x-term (b = 0); the constant is c = −9.

hints: Move all terms to one side.

topics.name: Factoring Method
topics.details: When a quadratic factors nicely, solving is fast. Put it in standard form, factor the left side, then use the zero-product rule: if a product equals zero, at least one factor is zero. So x² + 5x + 6 = 0 factors to (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, giving x = −2 or x = −3. For x² + bx + c, find two numbers multiplying to c and adding to b. Always factor out a common factor first. Factoring is the preferred SAT method whenever the roots are integers, because it is quicker and less error-prone than the formula.

solved.solution: Difference of squares: (x − 3)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −3.
Factor x: x(x + 2) = 0, so x = 0 or x = −2.

hints: Two numbers multiply to 10, add to 7.

topics.name: Square Root Method
topics.details: When a quadratic has no linear (x) term, or can be written as a square equal to a number, take square roots directly — remembering both signs. From x² = 25 you get x = ±5; from (x − 2)² = 9 you get x − 2 = ±3, so x = 5 or x = −1. Isolate the squared quantity first, then apply ±√ to both sides. If the number is negative, there are no real solutions. The square-root method is the quickest route for "pure" quadratics and for equations already in vertex-like form, both common on the SAT.

hints: Take square roots of both sides.

topics.name: Completing the Square
topics.details: Completing the square rewrites x² + bx + c as a perfect square plus a constant, which then solves by square roots and reveals the vertex. Take half of b, square it, and add and subtract it: x² + 6x = (x + 3)² − 9. To solve x² + 6x + 5 = 0, write (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = 0, so (x + 3)² = 4 and x = −1 or −5. The method works for any quadratic (divide by a first if a ≠ 1) and is the source of the quadratic formula. The SAT uses it to convert to vertex form and to solve when factoring is awkward.

solved.problem: Solve x² + 4x − 5 = 0 by completing the square.
Write x² − 2x + 1 as a perfect square.

unsolved.problem: Solve x² + 2x − 3 = 0 by completing the square.
Write x² + 8x + 16 as a perfect square.

topics.name: Quadratic Formula
topics.details: The quadratic formula solves any quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a). Substitute a, b and c with their signs, compute the discriminant b² − 4ac, then evaluate both roots. The discriminant also tells you how many real solutions there are: positive gives two, zero gives one (a repeated root), and negative gives none (no real solutions). Use the formula when factoring is hard or the roots are not integers. On the Digital SAT the built-in calculator handles the arithmetic, but knowing the formula and discriminant is essential for setup.

solved.problem: How many real solutions does x² + 2x + 5 = 0 have?

unsolved.problem: How many real solutions does x² − 6x + 9 = 0 have?
How many real solutions does x² + x + 1 = 0 have?
How many real solutions does x² − 2x − 3 = 0 have?
